2) Outage Occurrence/Duration Trend Over Years (Per FIPS)¶

The nvSRwVGPbmuu cell iterates through each tract_fips and performs OLS regression against the year column for both outage_occurrence and outage_duration_mean (after log transformation for duration). It then calculates significance flags and trend directions based on the results.

3) Month Effect in Each Year¶

Method: Chi-square goodness-of-fit per year, with expected monthly outages proportional to days in month. Then identify significantly high months by standardized residuals (FDR-corrected).

7) Add CVI Variables: Trend Slope Distribution + Exploratory Regression¶

This section starts to bring the CVI fields into the tract-year analysis. It does three things:

  1. builds a tract-level CVI table from Outage_CVI_Events.csv,
  2. looks at the distribution of tract trend slopes, and
  3. runs a few exploratory regression specifications with interactions and nonlinear terms.

8) Data Structure Check + More Intuitive County-Year Models¶

Important diagnostic: within each county-year, the outage measures in this merged file are identical across tracts. That means tract-level CVI regressions above should be read as replicated county outcomes rather than true tract-specific causal evidence.

A more intuitive next step is to collapse to a balanced county-year panel, summarize CVI at the county level, and fit count / duration models there.

9) Clean Model Family: One CVI Concept at a Time¶

This section directly implements the recommended next step. The goal is to reduce multicollinearity by fitting a small family of simpler county-year models, each with only one main CVI concept at a time.

For count outcomes, we compare both:

  • OLS on log1p(outage_occurrence)
  • Poisson GLM on raw outage_occurrence

Quick read: if the CVI coefficient keeps a similar sign across these simpler models, the relationship is more interpretable than in the multicollinear extended model.

In the cleaner county-year models, outage counts show a consistent positive relationship with time and, in most specifications, with severe weather exposure, suggesting that outage burden in NYC increased over the 2014-2023 period and generally rose with weather-related disruption. This pattern is stable across all 50 county-year observations in the balanced panel. Among the CVI measures, baseline social-economic vulnerability is the strongest and most interpretable predictor: in the OLS model, the coefficient on z_cvi_baseline_social_econ_mean is 0.444 with p = 0.015, and in the Poisson model the coefficient is 0.167 with an incidence rate ratio of 1.182, implying that a one-standard-deviation increase in county-level social-economic vulnerability is associated with roughly an 18% higher outage count. Overall CVI points in the same direction, with an OLS coefficient of 0.426 (p = 0.019) and a Poisson coefficient of 0.126 (IRR = 1.134), again indicating a positive association between broader vulnerability and outage burden. By contrast, the climate-extreme-events CVI measure is consistently negative across the cleaner models, with an OLS coefficient of -0.420 (p = 0.026) and a Poisson coefficient of -0.373 (IRR = 0.689), and the interaction model remains negative as well (-0.508, p < 0.001); because this sign is not especially intuitive, it should be treated cautiously rather than as a headline finding. The high-vulnerability-share variable is comparatively weak and not robust, with an OLS coefficient of 0.183 (p = 0.326) and a Poisson coefficient of -0.028 (p = 0.072). Taken together, these results suggest that the most defensible pattern in the data is a positive association between outage burden, time, severe weather, and especially social-economic vulnerability, while the evidence for other CVI dimensions remains more tentative.

Part 7 works best as an exploratory CVI extension of the original outage notebook: it merges the available tract-level CVI variables into the tract-year outage panel, examines the distribution of outage trend slopes, and tests richer OLS specifications with linear, interaction, and nonlinear terms. In that exploratory setup, the outage occurrence models appear to fit extremely well, with R² values from 0.651 to 0.684 across 20,993 observations, while the log-duration models have much weaker explanatory power, with R² only around 0.017-0.020, suggesting that CVI and weather variables line up much more strongly with outage counts than with outage duration. The coefficient table also points to potentially important CVI signals, especially around cvi_overall, cvi_baseline_social_econ, and cvi_climate_extreme_events, which is why this section is useful for hypothesis generation. However, Part 7 should not be treated as the notebook’s final inferential result, because the later county-year diagnostic shows that the outage outcomes in this merged file are repeated across tracts within the same county-year. So the main conclusion from Part 7 is that CVI looks promising, especially social-economic vulnerability, but these tract-level estimates are exploratory rather than definitive.

Part 8 is the key methodological correction in the notebook because it shows that the merged file behaves like a county-year outage dataset rather than a truly tract-specific outage panel. The diagnostic confirms that within each county-year, outage occurrence, mean outage duration, and severe-weather counts are identical across tracts, which means the tract-level regressions above were effectively reusing the same county-year outcomes many times. After collapsing to a balanced county-year panel with 50 county-year observations, the analysis becomes much more defensible. In the county summary, the Bronx stands out as the most socially vulnerable county, with cvi_overall_mean = 0.551 and cvi_baseline_social_econ_mean = 0.761, while Manhattan has the lowest overall vulnerability (0.446) and Staten Island has the highest climate-extreme-events mean (0.537). The county-level regressions suggest that outage burden rises over time and is positively related to vulnerability: in the basic count OLS model, year_centered = 0.156 (p = 0.015) and z_cvi_overall_mean = 0.426 (p = 0.019), while in the extended count OLS model z_cvi_baseline_social_econ_mean = 2.541 (p < 0.001) remains the strongest positive CVI correlate. The Poisson model tells a similar story, with year_centered = 0.087 (IRR = 1.091), z_severe_weather_count = 0.099 (IRR = 1.104), and z_cvi_baseline_social_econ_mean = 1.907 (IRR = 6.736). Duration remains less convincing: the duration OLS model has only R² = 0.117, and most predictors are weak except for a negative coefficient on z_cvi_climate_extreme_events_mean (-0.223, p = 0.039). Overall, Part 8 supports the conclusion that the strongest and most credible pattern in the notebook is a positive association between outage burden, time, severe weather, and especially county-level social-economic vulnerability, while duration results and some climate-CVI findings are much more tentative.

Part 9 provides the cleanest and most interpretable version of the CVI analysis by fitting a small family of county-year models in which only one main CVI concept is included at a time, directly addressing the multicollinearity problem documented in Part 8. This matters because the county-level CVI summaries are highly correlated with each other, for example cvi_overall_mean and cvi_overall_p75 correlate at 0.981, cvi_overall_mean and cvi_baseline_social_econ_mean at 0.902, and high_cvi_share and cvi_overall_p75 at 0.959, so extended models that include many of them at once are hard to interpret. In the cleaner one-CVI-at-a-time models, the most stable pattern is that outage counts remain positively associated with time and, in most cases, with severe weather, while social-economic vulnerability emerges as the strongest CVI signal. In OLS, z_cvi_baseline_social_econ_mean has a coefficient of 0.444 (p = 0.015), slightly stronger than z_cvi_overall_mean at 0.426 (p = 0.019), and both models have similar fit (R² = 0.295 and 0.289, respectively). In Poisson, the same ordering appears: z_cvi_baseline_social_econ_mean = 0.167 with IRR = 1.182 and p < 0.001, compared with z_cvi_overall_mean = 0.126 with IRR = 1.134 and p < 0.001, indicating that a one-standard-deviation increase in social-economic vulnerability is associated with roughly an 18% higher outage count. The climate-extreme-events measure behaves differently, showing a negative coefficient in both OLS (-0.420, p = 0.026) and Poisson (-0.373, IRR = 0.689), and remaining negative in the interaction model as well (-0.508, p < 0.001), which is not especially intuitive and should therefore be treated cautiously rather than highlighted as a substantive finding. The high-vulnerability-share measure is not robust, with an OLS coefficient of 0.183 (p = 0.326) and a Poisson coefficient of -0.028 (p = 0.072). Overall, Part 9 gives the clearest final message in the notebook: once the models are simplified and multicollinearity is reduced, the most consistent and interpretable relationship is a positive association between outage burden, time, severe weather, and especially county-level social-economic vulnerability, while the other CVI findings remain more tentative.

10) Duration-Focused County-Year Exploration¶

The earlier duration models relied mainly on county-year mean duration and produced relatively weak results. This section explores more interpretable duration outcomes based on deduplicated outage events within each county-year, including median duration, p90 duration, and the share of long outages.

The duration analysis was refined by moving from county-year mean duration to event-level, deduplicated outage records and then constructing more interpretable county-year duration outcomes, including median duration, p90 duration, and the shares of outages lasting more than 8 or 24 hours. This produced a panel of 47 county-year observations based on 4,518 unique outage events. The descriptive results show that typical outage durations in NYC are generally short, with county-year median durations often around 1-2 hours, while the upper tail can be substantially longer; for example, in the Bronx the median duration ranged from 1.0 to 2.25 hours across 2014-2023, while the p90 duration ranged from 1.625 to 13.2 hours. The share of outages lasting more than 8 hours was usually modest but clearly nonzero in some years, reaching 0.133 in the Bronx in 2020, whereas the share above 24 hours was much smaller and often close to zero. Across the duration-focused regression models, the clearest and most consistent predictor was the severe-weather event share, which had a positive coefficient in every specification and was especially strong for upper-tail duration outcomes such as p90 duration. By contrast, county-level CVI variables were much weaker and less stable predictors of outage duration than they were for outage counts. Taken together, these results suggest that in the current dataset vulnerability is more clearly associated with how many outages occur, while outage duration appears to depend more directly on weather severity and the characteristics of the outage events themselves.
